maintopic: ADJUSTMENTS IN PAYMENTS UNDER EMERGENCY GOLD MINING ASSISTANCE ACT

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ADJUSTMENTS IN PAYMENTS UNDER EMERGENCY GOLD MINING ASSISTANCE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the concurrence of my colleague, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), I wish to make a statement regarding gold.
Hon. members may recall that on December 27 last, a delegation representing the gold mining industry in all parts of Canada came to Ottawa and made representations to the Prime Minister and a group of his colleagues. These representations related to the prevailing difficult conditions in the industry resulting from the increasing cost of production in the face of a fixed price for the industry's product and included recommendations for various changes in legislation or policy designed to assist the industry in meeting

Gold Mining Assistance Payments the prevailing conditions and to avoid the closing down of mines with the hardship this would cause to a number of small northern communities largely or wholly dependent upon such mines.
As a result of the consideration given to these representations, the government had decided to consult with the international monetary fund in regard to arrangements which would make it possible for the industry to have access to premium markets for gold similar to the arrangements which the fund had agreed upon in the case of South Africa. To this end discussions were initiated with officers of the fund preparatory to the submission of a formal proposal to the executive board of the fund. We were then informed that the fund's staff was currently studying the situation arising out of the recent sharp increase in sales of gold in hoarding markets and had already decided to request the board to give urgent consideration to the whole question. Accordingly, the Canadian government was requested to defer the submission of a formal proposal pending this general review by the board. As a result of this review, the executive board of the fund passed the resolution which was made public on March 7.
For the convenience of hon. members, I think it would be desirable to place this resolution on Hansard. It reads as follows:
Since the amount of sales and purchases in the world markets of gold for jewelry, artistic and industrial purposes has recently been increasing at a rate indicating that at least a part of it finds its way to private hoards, contrary to the gold policy of the fund established in June, 1947, the board considers the existing arrangements and practices of several countries, including South Africa, are no longer a satisfactory basis to implement the fund's gold policy and directs the staff of that fund urgently to elaborate, after consultation with the countries concerned, more effective methods than the existing ones.
It appears from the resolution that the board considers the existing arrangements and practices of several countries, including South Africa, as no longer a satisfactory basis to implement the fund's gold policy. The Canadian government has endeavoured in this, as in other matters, to observe its international responsibilities, and in the case of its gold policy has had in mind the interests of establishing orderly international monetary arrangements and the maintenance of a sound position for gold in the future. Because of the desirability of close co-operation in many fields with our partners in this international emergency, and in the light of the new resolution passed by the fund, the government has decided not to alter the Canadian gold sales policy for the time being at least.

In view of this decision, the government has given further consideration to possible adjustments in the payments to be made under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act with a view to making some modifications which should more effectively assist the industry in overcoming the special difficulties with which it is confronted in the present circumstances.
It is now proposed to broaden the formula for the calculation of assistance payments during the calendar year 1951, which was announced on October 25 last by my colleague, the then minister of mines and technical surveys. This announcement stated that the government would introduce legislation at this session of parliament under which the rate of assistance in 1951 would be one-half of the amount by which the average cost of production per ounce of gold produced from any mine exceeds $22, provided that in no case should the rate of assistance exceed $11.50 per ounce. This rate of assistance was to be applied to the number of ounces of gold produced by a mine in excess of two-thirds of the number of ounces produced during the base year 1949, or one-third the number of ounces produced during 1951, whichever was the larger.
Under our present proposals no change will be made in the rate of assistance I have just described. However, it is now proposed that this rate of assistance will apply to the number of ounces of gold by which the number of ounces produced from the mine in the year 1951 and sold exceeds one-half of the number of ounces produced in the base year 1949 and sold. In no case, moreover, will the assistance payable be based on less than one-half the number of ounces produced from the mine during the present year and sold.
I do not, of course, wish to anticipate at this time the detailed explanation and discussion which my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys will wish to give the house when he introduces the proposed legislation. All I need add at this moment is that this modification in our gold assistance formula has been discussed with the fund, which has raised no objection.
In conclusion, may I express the belief that the new program which extends the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act on a modified basis to the year 1951 will be of further assistance to the industry generally in meeting rising costs of production and will enable the continued operation of many mines in northern communities wholly or largely dependent upon them.

speechtext:
Before the hon. member proceeds, may I say to the house that I have had some difficulty deciding whether the amendment to the amendment is in order. I have not yet come to a definite conclusion on this matter. From time to time the question arises in the house as to whether a motion involves an obligation on the part of the government to make an expenditure of money. Of course, if it does involve such an obligation on the part of the government, it is obviously out of order.
The amendment to the amendment proposes to amend the amendment by adding the following words:
It being the opinion of this house that consideration should be given to a final payment of twenty-five cents per bushel.
There has been a practice established in this house that private members may, by giving notice of motion framed in abstract and general terms, obtain the opinion of the house on matters involving the expenditure of money, or requesting that the government take into consideration the advisability of making such expenditure. It occurs to me that the situation might be different on the second reading of a bill. Although the words "that consideration should be given" are in the actual amendment, does that mean in practice that the government would be required to make the expenditure?
As I say, I think there is a difference between a private member's motion and a motion on second reading of a bill. If any hon. members would like to express their opinions on this subject, I should be glad to hear them.

speechtext:
-which I should like to call to your attention. First of all, citation 444 of BeaUiChesne's third edition consists of two paragraphs that I should like to read. I point out before doing so that the first paragraph deals with private members' motions that would seem to involve the expenditure

Canadian Wheat Board Act of money indirectly. The second paragraph deals with an amendment to a government piece of legislation. Your Honour has suggested that in your view there may be some difference on that score. I do not see how that distinction can be drawn as long as the wording of the amendment to a piece of government legislation makes it clear that it is expressing only an abstract opinion. Let me read citation 444. It is as follows:
Private members may introduce resolutions that do not directly Involve the expenditure of public money and have no operative effect but simply express an abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant.
Note the second paragraph, which reads:
An amendment-
In other words, an amendment to government legislation.
merely asserting as an abstract principle the expediency of a larger expenditure than that recommended by the crown in resolutions can be proposed, such amendment being moved mainly to prevent concurrence in the resolutions and having no practical effect with regard to public moneys unless the said increased expenditure is recommended by a new message from the crown.
It seems significant to me that those two paragraphs are right together in one citation, one of them dealing with private members' notices of motions and the other dealing with a motion amending a government measure.
I would also ask, Mr. Speaker, that you note three Speakers' decisions. They are lengthy, and I will not read them in full. One of them is reported on page 537 of Beau-chesne's third edition, a decision given by Mr. Speaker Rhodes on March 16, 1921, which reads:
Private members may introduce resolutions when they do not directly involve the expenditure of public money and have no operative effect but simply express an abstract opinion on a matter which may necessitate a future grant.
The two or three pages that follow that introduction indicate that the ruling was with reference to a private member's notice of motion. The same is true in the case of a ruling made by Mr. Speaker Sproule on February 1, 1912. You will find that one beginning on page 529, but if you will turn to page 519 of Beauchesne's third edition you will find a ruling by Mr. Speaker Cockburn, the introduction to which reads:
An amendment merely asserting as an abstract principle the expediency of a larger expenditure than that recommended by the crown in resolutions, can be proposed, such amendment being moved mainly to prevent concurrence in the resolution and having no practical effect with regard to public moneys unless the said increased expenditure is recommended by a new message from the crown.
If you will turn to pages 520 and 521 you will find that this amendment was moved by a Mr. Wood back in 1869. He wanted certain words left out and other words put in which
fMr. Knowles.]

expressed the opinion that such and such should not be done without at the same time making provision for increasing in due proportion, and on principles alike just to the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, the amount of debt allowed by the British North America Act to the late province of Canada, and so on. Further down on that page the Speaker, in giving his decision, said:
The motion of the hon. member for Brant is a mere assertion of an abstract principle. Beyond that, it proposes nothing; it does not propose to take any step in the direction of legislation, but, on the contrary, . . . the effect would be, if passed, to prevent concurrence in the resolutions, and to stop the whole proceedings-so that the question on this proposed appropriation could not be approached again, this session, unless a message came down from the crown recommending such additional expenditure. Therefore, I think the argument unsound that this amendment involves a question of additional public expenditure, and, in my opinion, the motion is in order.
The point I ask Your Honour to consider is that that ruling bears directly on the point Your Honour has raised. For my part, I cannot see the difference between a private member's notice of motion and a private member's amendment to government legislation so far as the question of involving an expenditure of money is concerned. Here is a clear-cut case where the amendment by a private member was to a government piece of legislation, and the Speaker ruled that, since the wording made it clear that it was abstract and did not have operative or legislative effect, it was in order.
I point out that the wording of the amendment to the amendment moved by my desk-mate, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), is clearly in abstract form. It is governed in the first place by the wording in the earlier part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross), which merely says that further consideration of this bill should be deferred until consideration has been given to such-and-such. Then my colleague's amendment proposes the addition of the words:
It being the opinion of this house that consideration should be given to a final payment of twenty-five cents per bushel.
If I were to take more time, which I will not, I could point out to Your Honour several cases in which motions were allowed which did not even include the word "consideration," because it was clear that they simply expressed the opinion of the house. My colleague's amendment not only uses the words, "it being the opinion of this house," but goes on to say merely that consideration should be given to the proposal indicated in the subamendment.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because of the proper wording of my colleague's amendment, and because of the citations I have called to Your Honour's attention, particularly the words of Mr. Speaker Cockburn as recorded on page 521 of Beauchesne's third edition, I submit that the amendment to the amendment is in order.

I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for your decision to permit the subamendment to stand.
Last evening when I was discussing this matter I was about to point out that the farmers of western Canada were not basing their claim for a greater payment than the 83 cents the government has announced upon whether there was a period or a comma in a particular sentence the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) might have spoken in this house. Their claim for some further consideration under the "have regard to" clause has a much broader basis than that.
We also had some argument yesterday as to whether any final agreement was reached on the "have regard to" clause, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that when he vas in England in May he did not reach any
Canadian Wheat Board Act final agreement with the British government but that he brought back a report to the cabinet. He stated yesterday, at page 1072 of Hansard, "I reported that position to them"- that is, the position taken by the British government. "The decision, if there was any decision, was made after I returned." Until we have the minutes of proceedings and the communications between the British government and the Canadian government on this matter we are not in a position to say definitely whether the cabinet reached a decision and accepted the position the British government had taken with regard to the "have regard to" clause. That is why we are anxious to have these papers tabled at the earliest possible moment. As a matter of fact we should have had them before this discussion took place. Then we would be able to reach an intelligent decision based upon the actual documents that passed between the two governments.
Another reason we believe we are entitled to a further and larger payment than 8 [DOT] 3 cents is the fact that for two years, from 1945 to 1947, Canadian consumers were supplied with 160 million bushels of wheat at $1.25 a bushel, when the price received under the British contract was $1.55. Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made quite a point of the fact that the average price at which wheat was sold outside of the British contract over the five year period was $1.82 a bushel. That low average only resulted from the fact that through the wheat board the Canadian government sold 160 million bushels to the domestic trade in Canada at $1.25 a bushel, which was below the price under the British contract and which represented a loss to the wheat producers of western Canada of some $48 million.
Many people will say that many other producers in Canada were in the same position during those years; and I want to point out that those were years after the war was over, 1945 to 1947, when we were selling this wheat to the Canadian consumer at $1.25 a bushel. There were restrictions on the people selling lumber, steel, pulp and other materials. But I point out that so far as I know there was no other material in Canada over which the government had taken complete control. In no other case did the government take all the product and then go out and sell it in the name of the producers. The people who produced pulp, steel, lumber or other products were given a free hand under the ceiling prices that may have existed. They were able to sell their products within Canada at whatever they could get for them under those ceilings. Most of the ceiling prices were removed in 1946 and 1947, and they were allowed to sell their products in the Canadian
1080	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act market at the highest prices they could obtain. They were also permitted to sell the share of their products they were exporting at the highest prices they could obtain in the export market, not under a contract such as we had with Great Britain, which to all intents and purposes placed a ceiling on the price.
These are some of the reasons why people in western Canada believe they are entitled to a payment of more than 8-3 cents. The government failed to maintain a price ceiling in this country. In this house the Minister of Agriculture stated that the producer was protected under the wheat board act, just as other producers were protected under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Let me indicate just what that meant. The minister stated that in determining the prices for agricultural products under that act consideration would be given to the fact that during the first two or three years of the war agricultural prices in some cases were below the cost of production. When the ceilings were placed on agricultural prices in the fall of 1941 in many cases those prices were below the cost of production, and the minister said that in determining prices under the Agricultural Prices Support Act that matter would be taken into consideration. At page 5624 of Hansard for July 29, 1944, the minister is reported as having said:
I was careful to see that there was nothing In the bill which said that we were going to base any decision on the cost of production. The cost of production may be only part of the consideration. X think it is possible the board might determine that the farmer should have considerably more than his cost of production because of some other experience he has had in order to get through the transitional period in a proper position.
I ask the farmers of Canada to consider that statement. In setting the prices under the prices support act, in setting the final payment under the wheat board act, has the minister given consideration to the fact that in 1940, 1941 and 1942 the wheat producers of Canada were selling wheat for approximately 50 to 60 cents a bushel on the farm? That was approximately the average price for the average grade of wheat for the first three years of the war. I do not think 8-3 cents a bushel represents any consideration of that fact.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been amused by the discussions that have taken place on Bill No. 5 concerning the amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. So far as this party is concerned, we intend, at the proper time, to support the amendments proposed by the bill, which are three in number. The first one is apparently intended to correct an error, and changes the date of the commencement of the pool year from August 31 to August 1. Apparently the error was made when the bill was printed. The second concerns the adjustment of interim payments on different grades of grain. This is necessary because it is impossible to set initial payments at their proper level until some experience has been had by the board in selling those different grades. The third
Canadian Wheat Board Act concerns the transfer of wheat from one year's pool to another. I believe that is one that will be appreciated by the farmers all over the prairie provinces, because it will enable the wheat board to wind up its business year much faster and give the farmers a chance to use their own money rather than pay interest for a year or two on money that rightfully belongs to them but still remains in the wheat board's funds.
I have no intention whatever of chasing through the volumes of Hansard in order to follow up the quotations that the Minister of Agriculture made last night from his own speech. There are one or two items in his speech of last night which I should like to comment upon. The first is to be found at page 1059 of Hansard, in the first column, where he said:
We make all kinds of claims, which I am not going to take the trouble to make here tonight, as to what the result of the inauguration of the policy has been; but I recite this in order to repeat that the farmers of western Canada have absolute confidence in the co-operative organizations that they set up to handle their grain, and there is no kind of argument that is going to be put up by anyone in this house to the effect that somebody has lost a lot of money that is going to change the attitude of the farmers of western Canada toward the system that they themselves have set up. They are going to operate under that system, and anyone making speeches from this house with the idea that he is going to encourage some change by saying that the farmers have lost $300 million or $600 million, as the notion takes him when he is speaking, is wasting his time. I just want to say to them that they had better talk with some of the farmers in western Canada before making such speeches because there is nobody in western Canada that believes them.
In connection with that, lest there be any mistake about where I stand, I should like to say that I joined the Alberta wheat pool in early September of 1923. I was one of the first to sign a contract in my territory. I helped to organize the pool, and I am still a member of that organization. I still have thousands of bushels in the five-year pool, and up to today I believe I have delivered ninety-eight per cent of the grain I grew to the wheat pool elevator. I was a supporter of the wheat board at the time it was set up, and until it was finished after the first war. Had we been allowed to keep that wheat board, there would not have been any need for setting up wheat pools. Because we were denied that right we went ahead and organized our own wheat pools. I want to say that I am a firm believer in the wheat board, and in the wheat pools. While I am a member here it is my intention to support the wheat board. I believe we have an organization that has done a good job for the farmers. So far as I know there are no farmers dissatisfied with the work of the

Canadian Wheat Board Act wheat board. The figures I hope to give a little later will prove that beyond any question.
Then on page 1069 we find this-I am quoting the Minister of Agriculture:
The act may require further amendment from time to time; but in my opinion the farmers of the west have not been convinced that they have lost money under the system of wheat board marketing as compared with any other system.
I agree with that statement; but I am sure that most of the complaint has come about because of a deal that the Canadian government made with the British government, and because of the Canadian government's policy in supplying wheat at below regular price to Canadian millers so that Canadian consumers could eat cheap bread.
As to dissatisfaction among the people in the west-and reference was made to that matter by the minister last night-I am going to read something that was said by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture when they appeared here on the fifteenth of last month:
1.	We wish to express our appreciation of the efforts of the government to obtain from Great Britain adequate recognition of the "have regard" clause in the Canadian-United Kingdom wheat agreement.
2.	We wish to point out that the government of Canada has a vital responsibility to see that wheat producers are treated fairly in the final settlement of the five-year pool, because the returns to wheat producers for those years were prescribed by government policy of sale of wheat in the domestic market and by the terms of the contract which the government made with the government of the United Kingdom in 1946.
Our wheat producers feel that balance of the actual proceeds of the sales of wheat during the five-year pool is not sufficient to provide a satisfactory settlement. Our convention was unanimous in asking that a very substantial contribution per bushel should be made by the government of Canada to the final settlement of the five-year pool.
Then again we had statements by the representatives of the three wheat pools at Regina early this week. We know what their opinion has been. Only yesterday the Alberta legislature passed a resolution favouring some worth-while final settlement of this five-year pool. In addition to that, I believe that many hon. members in all parts of the house have received letters and telegrams ever since the session started, pressing for a worth-while settlement of the five-year pool.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made a statement the other day-it was on Friday last-in connection with the final payment, people all over the country were greatly disappointed; but I believe no citizen was more disappointed than was the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). While the Prime Minister was making that statement
rMr. Fair.]
I watched the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who sat at his right, and the Minister of Agriculture, who sat at his left; and they were not a happy pair. It might seem fitting that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is in charge of that department, should make the announcement; or again, if he did not want to do it, it might seem proper that the Minister of Agriculture should do it, as he had quite a bit to do with the negotiations from start to finish. But perhaps neither of them wanted to make it; it was such a crumb from the rich man's table that neither of them wanted to hand it out, and the job fell to the lot of the Prime Minister.
For many years our Canadian wheat has been sold at prices that have been far below its actual value. Going back to February 25, 1947, we find this stated here in the house by the then minister of trade and commerce in connection with the sale of some of our wheat; and at that time-and in fact even prior to that time, in 1945-we had a ceiling of $1.55 a bushel placed upon our wheat, even though that figure was far below the value of that commodity. We find that the then minister of trade and commerce-at that time Hon. J. A. MacKinnon-as reported at page 787 of Hansard, set out in part a directive to the wheat board, as embodied in an order in council:
Whereas the Minister of Trade and Commerce reports that because of the effects of a crop failure in Australia and French North Africa, of transportation difficulties in various supplying countries, and of other adverse developments upon the volume of exportable wheat and because of the urgent requirements of recently liberated areas of Europe and Asia, world demand for wheat is presently exceeding available supplies;
That under these conditions Canada, as the principal wheat exporting country, is in a position to demand very much higher prices for wheat from importing countries which must obtain food from abroad regardless of price in order to avoid want and starvation and to many of which Canada has been or will be extending loans for rehabilitation and reconstruction purposes.
Shortly after that, we find that an agreement was made with Britain, that negotiations were going on for some time, as also were negotiations dealing with an international wheat agreement. But on July 25, 1946, the then minister of trade and commerce-again Mr. MacKinnon-announced an agreement with the British government. It must be pointed out that this agreement was one between the Canadian government and the British government and was not one made by the Canadian wheat board. Under the terms of the agreement Canada agreed to supply Britain with 160 million bushels out of the 1946-47 crop at a price of $1.55 a bushel. Ultimately we find that deliveries turned out to be 169 million bushels at $1.55;

and during that crop year the average price of class II wheat was $2.43 a bushel. Therefore the Canadian farmers who delivered that wheat had a loss of 88 cents per bushel, or a total of $148,720,000 on that wheat delivered. In the 1947-48 crop year we had agreed to deliver 160 million bushels at $1.55. Actual deliveries turned out to be 170-6 million. The average price of class II wheat during that year was $2.88 a bushel, so that the farmers lost an average of $1.33 a bushel, or a total loss of $226,898,000. In the third year of the agreement, the 1948-49 crop year, when we were supposed to deliver 140 million bushels, we actually delivered 146,342,802 bushels at a negotiated price of $2 per bushel. During that crop year the average price of class II wheat was $2.23 a bushel. Canadian farmers, therefore, suffered a loss of 23 cents a bushel, or a total of $33,658,844. In the last year of the contract, 1949-50, we delivered 140 million bushels; the negotiated price was $2 a bushel. The average price of class II wheat during that year was $2.16. There was therefore a loss per bushel to the Canadian farmer of 16 cents, or a total of $22,400,000. Those four figures total $431,676,844.
On August 14, 1946, when discussing this matter, as spokesman for this party I had this to say as reported at page 4800 of Hansard of that date:
On behalf of this group I wish to say that we are glad to know that we are to have stabilized prices for the next four crop years and also that an agreement has been made with Britain. I am not going to say whether we are well satisfied with the prices received. We feel that the British government are satisfied that they got a very good deal at the expense of Canada. One of my reasons for saying that is contained in a Canadian press dispatch of July 26, which states:
"The News-Chronicle's streamer headline said: Strachey explains wheat deal and M.P.'s cheer Canada."
In my opinion they had every right to cheer Canada. The dispatch goes on to say:
"The Mirror headlined the story: 'Pact makes Britain's loaf safe for four years.'
The Daily Graphic said editorially: 'Our debt to the empire increases every day . . . thanks, Canada, and thanks again!' "
I am glad the people of Britain appreciate that they are getting a good deal from Canada. I might say we have no objection whatever to Canada's supplying the best food in the world to Britain and to other countries, but we object to the farmers bearing the brunt of the expense. On many occasions we have made it clear that the farmers of Canada have not received the price for their products to which they are justly entitled. I still estimate that the same condition continues under the present agreement. Of course we are very well satisfied to have a stabilized price for some time to come, because we all remember what happened after the first great war and we do not want conditions of that kind to arise again; but in view of the losses the farmers accepted from 1930 up to 1942, I feel we are entitled to a much better deal as far as our wheat is concerned. I am not going to deal in particular with the sale to the British govern-
Canadian Wheat Board Act ment. The cost of that will, of course, be taken care of by the government here, and we in turn will have to bear our share of the loss through taxation.
Then at a later time the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), speaking with respect to a further amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, said1 on February 24, 1947, as reported at 746 of revised Hansard:
I believe that the wheat agreement with Britain was fully justified but it does entail in its early stages a considerable sacrifice on the part of our farmers. We feel that the sacrifice should be borne by the people of Canada as a whole, and that is why we are so concerned about the guarantee that the government makes regarding the acceptance of fourteen bushels to the acre, which is supposed to remove the sacrifice from the farmers and place the burden squarely on the backs of the Canadian people.
In addition to that we find that at that time the price of wheat was climbing. There were discussions throughout the country, and some discussion in the house as to losses that might be suffered by the farmers. But we were continually given to understand that the "have regard to" clause of the agreement would take care of that. The "have regard to" clause was referred to frequently yesterday, and; once today. When it came to fixing the price for the third year of the contract it was fixed at $2 per bushel, and did not take into consideration any of the losses that had been suffered by Canadian farmers during the first two years of that contract. It amounted to a loss of 88 cents a bushel in the first year and $1.33 a bushel in the second year, while in the third: year of the contract we suffered a loss of 23 cents a bushel. When it came to negotiating the price in the fourth year, the price was again set at $2, through negotiation between the two governments, and we lost on that 16 cents a bushel, as compared with the price of class II wheat. So that I feel there was no regard whatsoever to the "have regard" clause in. the agreement.
When people were getting anxious about their final payment we were told that final settlement would be made ini the middle of the summer. Before that time arrived we continued to supply to Canadian millers, for consumption by Canadian consumers throughout the country, certain quantities of wheat. In the early part of 1946-47 we supplied 29,041,927 bushels at a price of $1.25. The average price of class II wheat was $2.43, and therefore the loss per bushel was $1.18, which was absorbed by the farmers. Then, late in 1946-47 the price had risen to $1.55. We supplied a further 24,573,939 bushels. During that time the average price of class II wheat was $2.43, and therefore the loss was 88 cents a bushel.
In the first part of the year 1946-47 there was a net loss of $34,269,474, and for the

Canadian Wheat Board Act second quantity in that year a loss of $21,625,066. In the 1947-48 crop year we supplied the millers 49,342,532 bushels at a price of $1.55. The average price then was $2.88, and in that year there is a loss of $1.33 per bushel to the farmer. This amounted to a net loss of $65,625,567. In the 1948-49 crop year we supplied 39,281,098 bushels at a price of $2 per bushel. The class II price in that year was $2.23, and therefore there was a loss of 23 cents a bushel, making a total net loss in that year of $9,034,652. In the last year of the contract, 1949-50, we supplied 39,788,512 bushels, at a price of $2. As the average price of class II wheat was $2.16 we suffered a loss of 16 cents a bushel, or in that year a total net loss of $6,366,162.
These figures indicate a total bushelage of 182,028,008, with a loss in dollars of $136,920,921. To this must be added the loss on the British contract for the four-year period, making a total net loss of $568,597,765. Out of this the government announcement says that the farmers will be paid $120 million, so that there will remain a net loss to
be accounted for of $448,597,765. And instead of the 8-3 cents per bushel there should be a payment of approximately 40 cents to make up that loss.
If one were to average this loss among the average number of farmers who have taken out delivery permits that loss would amount on an average to $1,930 per wheat farmer. So that I feel there is something here to complain about, so far as the farmers of western Canada are concerned.
I have these figures before me in tabulated form. I might point out that they are taken chiefly from information brought down in sessional papers. The average prices for the first three crop years of the agreement were obtained from the 1948-49 Canadian wheat board report. The calculations I have made myself, and I feel they are quite correct. With the permission of hon. members I should like to place the table on Hansard.

It would appear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) feels that we should not bear all the loss, as far as cheap wheat to millers is concerned. In Hansard of August 14, 1946, as reported at page 4806, the minister said: Having said that, may I say that farm organizations generally, the farmers in particular, and most of us who represent wheat-growing constituencies in this house have always questioned the advisability of charging the farmer up with the difference between whatever the price was and the price at which wheat was being supplied to the millers. In other words, it should be emphasized over and over again that every banker, every operator, 
every railroad, every clerk in a bank or store, every labourer, every farmer has been buying flour, or his bread to put it in other terms, on the basis of 78-cent wheat ever since control came into effect in this country. In other words, we have been supplying that important food product to the people of this country, to the labouring people and consumers generally, at a lower rate than it is supplied anywhere else in the world. I agree with those who say that that whole cost should not be charged up to the farmer, and in discussions in the past I have maintained that too much of that cost has been charged up to the farmer. I still maintain that we should get away from that just as soon as we possibly can.

I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) still has the interests of agriculture at heart. While we have to have inflicted upon us a Liberal government I would much rather see the minister here as Minister of Agriculture that have him relegated to the other end of the building.

what used to be called the rump, but I am not quite finished with the Minister of Agriculture. In order to settle the argument that has been carried on between the Country Guide and the Winnipeg Free Press, perhaps I should read again from the October, 1950, issue. The Minister of Agriculture is not the only one who has been reading Hansard because I believe it has been thumbed through quite a bit during the past few weeks. I am going to read from the revised edition, which must be correct. Speaking on February 28, 1947, as reported on page 898 of Hansard, the minister said:
Now I come down to the last week before the British agreement was signed, when we knew all the facts with regard to it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and I met-I have stated this in the pool board meetings in western Canada and I have their consent to state it anywhere-we met the representatives of all the farmers' grain handling organizations in western Canada-the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Manitoba wheat pool, the Alberta wheat pool, the United Grain Growers. These organizations were all present, together with the president and secretary of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and a representative of the wheat growers of Ontario. The meeting was held for the purpose of discussing what the initial payment ought to be following this agreement. We were in a position at that time to inform them what that British agreement was, because it had all been agreed to. The agreement was signed I think two days later.
That should set at rest any doubt with regard to the discussions that took place on that occasion. It has been said that all these organizations had given consent to the British wheat agreement, but that is not the case. They were called in for an entirely different purpose. While we were giving the consumers of Canada cheap wheat so that they could eat cheap bread and thus have a better standard of living than the farmers who were growing the wheat-I might mention that most people in towns and cities have bathrooms, electric light and all that kind of thing, when only a small percentage of the farmers who grew the wheat have these conveniences-we were forced to pay higher prices for everything we bought. I do not blame labour for getting a reasonable wage, but I feel that we should not be asked to stand this loss.	[DOT]
I feel the Minister of Agriculture has been trying to do a good job. The Western Producer 80709-70
Canadian Wheat Board Act of November 13, 1950, contains the following report with regard to the convention of the Saskatchewan wheat pool:
Expressing the view that there was still a large body of public opinion in Great Britain that felt that Canada was entitled to further payments under the adjustment clause of the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement, Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, federal minister of agriculture, told wheat pool delegates that the matter was still under discussion.
Mr. Gardiner was speaking at the twenty-sixth annual meeting of delegates, policy forming body of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Earlier in the week delegates also heard an address by the Right Hon. C. D. Mr. Gardiner, in reviewing some of the marketing history relating to wheat, pointed out that prior to the date of the contract between the United Kingdom and Canadian governments,-

speechtext: The matter of the "have regard to" clause was discussed in great detail during our sessions with Sir Stafford Cripps and other ministers of the United Kingdom government. speechtext:
Instead of the Minister of Trade and Commerce going to Britain last year many people felt that it would! have been appropriate' had the Minister of Agriculture gone. Some feel that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not the right one to go. If he does not have more success in his deals in the future than he had in extracting a few more pennies from the British government then I think he had better send the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). These little fellows do not seem to care how big the other fellow is. They think that the bigger he is the harder he falls. I feel that the Minister of Agriculture is interested in his department. He knows his department. He believes in the wheat board, as I do, and I believe that he should have the sale of wheat in his department. I am not going to discuss that point further because my time is running out. Perhaps I should have cut my remarks down quite a bit.
I say that the wheat growers of the prairie provinces are not asking for a handout. They are simply demanding the same price as was obtained by the wheat board for class II wheat. That does not mean wheat sold through the Chicago market or any other

market. We are asking for the same price as was obtained for class II wheat sold by the Canadian wheat board. The prices obtained by the wheat board for such wheat should be sufficient evidence that the board has done an excellent job, and that they have an excellent chairman, deputy chairman and commissioners, So far as I am concerned, I do not want to leave any doubt whatever as to where I stand in connection with this matter.
The advocates of the grain exchange are using the results under the British wheat agreement as an argument for throwing the wheat board out of business. In my opinion that is poor business on their part. Perhaps they are doing that because for a number of years I have advocated that they be thrown out of the grain exchange and made to earn an honest living. I still feel that they are carrying on in a dishonest way, and are trying to further their interests by attempting to pin on the wheat board the bad parts of the British wheat agreement. I feel quite safe in saying that if legislation to continue the wheat board in operation is not passed you will have one of the biggest farmers' strikes in western Canada that the country has ever experienced.
Since the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made his statement about the settlement of the wheat agreement many supporters of the government have been blaming the socialists in Great Britain. They say that if the darn socialists had paid their debts the government would be able to make a much better payment. I think that is entirely a matter between the Canadian and British governments. So far as this group is concerned, we feel the whole responsibility of making these losses good rests fairly and squarely on the doorstep of the Canadian government. In the interests of Canada as a whole, I believe that the demands for payment should be honoured. Labour cannot get along without agriculture. In the Rural Co-Operator of January 24, 1950, there is a report of an address by Mr. C. H. Millard, director of the United Steelworkers of America, to the annual meeting of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture held in Toronto recently. The report reads in part:
"Falling farm prices", said Mr. Millard, "are giving all of us grave concern. We know that when farm prices fall below an economic level unemployment is going to follow, and we fear the future under such conditions. Frankly, I am a little concerned over the loose thinking of the past few years about the markets for our so-called exportable surpluses . . . The standard of life everywhere must be raised, here in Canada as well as abroad, so that labour is able to buy the goods the farmer produces, and the farmer can buy ours."
It is a two-way business. We must not do anything to destroy the purchasing power of the farmer, and we must also see to it

that labour has work to do. We feel that the farmers must be treated like human beings. References have been made with pride to the great strides the industrial life of Canada has made. I feel, as I have said on many other occasions, that we cannot have a prosperous and united Canada with part of our people well off and enjoying a high standard of living while others are in poverty.
When I spoke on the 6th of February I stated that facts that are not frankly faced have a habit of stabbing us in the back. I state that again today because when the international wheat agreement was introduced in the house we did not favour it with any great enthusiasm. Prices were cut down from what we had been receiving prior to that time so far as class II wheat was concerned. In order to try to get some safeguard, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), who is always sound in his thinking and in the speeches he makes, wanted to have the price of wheat tied to the prices of goods in other countries so that if there was a fluctuation in the prices of goods the price of wheat would fluctuate with them.
That suggestion was not even answered, or apparently considered, by the government. We now see the price of wheat going down while the prices of the products the farmer has to buy in order to produce are continually climbing. That is one of the results. First of all the wheat farmers want a reasonable and decent settlement of the British wheat agreement, and with respect to the wheat supplied to millers for Canadian consumption. Then farmers will be ready to go to work again. It has been pointed out that we are in a state of grave peril at the present time. Do not forget that regardless of the efficiency and prosperity of our industries we cannot get along without the farmer. If the farmer is not properly treated, do not forget that he can refuse to co-operate just as the industrialists did in 1939 when they would not work until the five per cent profit limitation was removed.
Do not forget that farmers are not as dumb as a lot of people think they are. In order to make things much better for all Canadians, I again suggest that a policy guaranteeing parity prices to agriculture should be put into effect without further delay. At the present time farmers comprise about 25 per cent of the population of Canada, and according to the best information that we can get from the financial branch of the bureau of statistics farmers are receiving somewhere between 10 and 15 per cent of the national income, one-half of what we are properly entitled to.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). I hope I shall be excused if I do not agree with all his political philosophy. However, I can agree with his last sentence or two when he said that the industrial and agricultural life of Canada are closely associated. I realize that when the one is prosperous it has an interlocking effect on the other. I am sure that every hon. member realizes that there is no time when the interests of industry and agriculture are more interlocking and of more vital concern than during a time such as we are passing through at present. I am satisfied that at no time in the history of Canada have a strong agricultural population and industry been of more vital concern than now when we are facing a possible world conflict. It was our strong agricultural position that assisted so much in the first great war, and indeed it was our strong agricultural industry that assisted so greatly in the second great war. I know we await with considerable concern, if not alarm, what may happen in the next few years as to the part agriculture may be called upon to play.
I am not going to depart from the issue now before the house. I followed the remarks of the hon. member for Battle River and I can agree with him to a large extent when he says that production in many branches of Canadian agriculture has been seriously affected and vitally weakened as we face a possible world conflict. That has come about, I believe, to no small extent through unsound policies practised by this government which since confederation has boasted of being the champion of laissez-faire, free enterprise, business as usual, individual recompense for individual effort, free trade, and all the other things that go with a free man who does not care what happens as long as it does not happen to him.
The minister has been a sturdy champion of a new form of bulk trading; but I cannot understand why he should be such a champion of free enterprise for almost every industry in Canada except the great industry of agriculture, which he represents in this house. At one time I think he was a free trader. Like many others of his party he has changed a great deal since that time. I believe in many respects he has always been more or less a champion of free enterprise; and I have heard him speak loudly and long of the economic freedom that resulted in Canada from these policies of his party. I recall that back in 1941 he brought in a policy under which the farmers of western Canada were paid not to grow wheat at all on certain

Canadian Wheat Board Act acres. That policy was accepted by this government, though I think he had some trouble in selling it to some of his colleagues and more than a little trouble selling it to the house. And I remember that famous summer fallow policy that came into operation in the first few years of the last war. We criticized that policy at that time, though wheat prices were low; and it was not long before many parts of the world were starving for wheat.
I could never conceive how the minister was able to sell his bulk trading policy in 1946 to his colleagues in the cabinet, especially the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I can only assume that that right hon. gentleman was so busy straightening out war assets, destroying old military equipment and trying to get this country back to normal civil production that he was not paying very much attention to these bulk trading policies in which his department would later find itself so involved in its administration.
I well recall that many on this side of the house proclaimed as vigorously as they could that this bulk trading policy was unsound in practice and would be a colossal blunder in the marketing of our wheat. I remember that at that time the Minister of Agriculture pleaded with us in this house to stand behind him in this venture, saying that we would try this experiment and see what happened. Some of us prophesied that it would lose millions of dollars to our farmers. Some of us suggested that it was unsound business practice to sell a man something today for less than its value and expect him five years later to pay you more for your product than he would have to pay in another market. I am a farmer, like the minister. I have done a little business around the farm occasionally. I have traded a few horses now and then. If in 1924 I sold a man something for much less than it was worth he would probably invite me to dinner when I met him at the local hotel, and would tell anyone around to vote for me because I was a good fellow; but he would not come back in 1930 and pay me more than a similar product was worth. Business is not done in that way. The British are smart business people. I always had my doubts as to what would happen. I feel almost like saying "I told you so," because I felt this would be the result.
What is the position after four or five years of this bulk trading? I am not going into the details, because I did not take much time to prepare my remarks. I was so astounded by some of the statements made yesterday by the right hon. Minister of Agriculture, however, that I felt impelled to

say a few words today on this very important issue. We have confused our relationship with the British purchasers of wheat, and we have antagonized other countries who wanted our wheat at the time and had to pay more for it. We have dislocated the whole market for our principal agricultural product by selling part of it for less than it was worth and the rest at world market prices. I sometimes wonder how anyone with sound business judgment could have expected anything else. I am sure no one within the sound of my voice who has had experience in the industrial life of this nation would expect to be able to carry on business in that way and maintain good relationships with his customers. That is not done by selling Jones the product at one price and Smith the same product at half as much again. Business is just not done in that way.
I think the Britishers saw the Minister of Agriculture coming. They probably said to themselves that while he belonged to a free enterprise party in Canada, so-called, nevertheless he had caught the fever from some of his western friends who believe that someone else can run your business better than you can run it yourself. Whatever changed him so he would think bulk trading was the only way we could sell our wheat is still one of the question marks in this whole transaction.
Today the responsibility is with the government, with their large majority in this house. The unfairness of this situation is obvious to everyone. We have the western wheat grower humbly begging the government of Canada to make up to him the loss that must have seemed inevitable to anyone who carefully studied the proposition. On the other side of the picture we have the government suggesting that the taxpayers, the widows, the workingmen and all the rest who contribute to the consolidated revenue fund, must pay through taxation for this colossal error in the marketing of this great Canadian product. I would say that I am trying to tell you what your party has done and what it has not done. When these agreements were negotiated, Mr. Speaker, we were told we were going to receive a lower price than the world price, but that that would be taken care of by the "have regard to" clause and in the end the farmer would receive more money. I am not going to go into that in any detail. I have not got a lot of detail here. I have only a few notes that I scribbled a few minutes before I entered the chamber. I only wish that I had a staff like some of the government members that would furnish me with more material, because I think I could make it a lot more

interesting. I do know that the Winnipeg Free Press, which has not told many untruths about the historic Liberal party for some years, and which is considered to be one of the finest newspapers in this dominion, says there has been a loss of at least $330 million.
I know it is a fine newspaper, and one which I would rather have with me than against me. I have been trying for years to get it with me. That newspaper sets the figure at $330 million.

The member for Calgary East
(Mr. Harkness) says that is for the first two years. I notice that other members have set this figure much higher. I studied it quite carefully during the election campaign, and I made it much higher myself. I know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) knows I have been long enough in public life that I will not lie to my constituents. I am not going to say whether the loss today is half a billion dollars or $750 million. I do believe that the muddling and meddling in Canadian agricultural products by this government has cost the farmers, before income taxes, at least a billion dollars.
The Minister of Agriculture said some time ago that we were trying an experiment. I must say that, doubtful even as I have been of this type of policy, one could not observe the adroit, smooth political ability of the Minister of Agriculture without at least giving him some credit for having possibilities as a good businessman. At that time we said, "Well, he is smart, perhaps not only in parliament but at least in the country, he has fooled more electors than any other minister of agriculture we ever had." I have often thought that my friends down to the left are pretty good, but I think that when it comes to convincing the farmers, especially a small group of them who believe in it, the Minister of Agriculture can convince an honest farmer against his will with more success than any other politician I have known in the last quarter of a century. The mere fact there is a young farmer in my riding or in the Minister of Agriculture's riding who says he is satisfied to take X dollars for his wheat in the next five years does not guarantee that this is a sound economic policy. I say with all due respect to the Minister of Agriculture, and to you, Mr. Speaker, that this policy has been a colossal failure.
If I had not thought it was a colossal failure before, I would have known it was when, from behind the curtain last evening, I heard the Minister of Agriculture's voice, because I have heard him for so many years,
Canadian Wheat Board Act and I know him so well, that whenever I see that little champion of Liberalism in Canada getting out in the aisle and speaking more loudly and longer than he usually does,
I know he has a difficult case to put over. That has been proven down through the years. For his debating skill I should like to compliment him, and his party. I know he loves parliamentary debate much better than does the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I do not mean to say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not forceful in the house, although I think he is more forceful outside the house. I do not think he likes debating quite as well as the Minister of Agriculture. I can understand why the rest of the Liberal party, whenever there is a difficult job to do, will sit quietly and leave it to their little champion, because he is the best in this parliament when the going is tough, and the going was never tougher than it was last night.
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the figures representing the loss are a legend in Canada now. The Winnipeg Free Press has used much ink and newsprint in publishing them in the last few years and has tried vigorously to explain the true picture. In doing so I believe they did a grand service, because the figures will get into the hands of young farmers who will look them over. It is all very fine to say, Mr. Speaker-and it is a trick as old as this parliament itself-that the prices for farm products today are higher. They say "Look, the farmer received $500 million more this year than last year; he received more for wheat than the year before. What were agricultural prices in 1932?" I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I have farmed quite steadily; in fact my family have been farmers for the past three or four generations. I can well recall when we sold wheat for $1.25 a bushel and barley for 96 cents. But then we bought a binder to cut the grain for $110. It is true we now sell wheat for $1.55 or more as may be fixed by this government with the socialistic turn of mind, but we are now paying as high as $800 for a binder. Threshing machines that could have been bought three or four years ago for $1,100 now cost $2,300. I shall not go down the line because there is not a farmer within the sound of my voice who does not know that the cost of almost every farm implement has practically doubled.
Turning now to farm labour costs, Mr. Speaker, at the time wheat was a dollar a bushel just before the first great war, labour costs were much lower. Compare them with today's labour costs. I am not familiar with what the farmers of western Canada are paying, because I have not discussed it with

Canadian Wheat Board Act them. I have a fair idea of what they would have to pay in view of the industries that are competing with them. I know that in our district the average farmer is paying, and I presume this is general throughout Ontario because there is a fair amount of industry around Waterloo and St. Catharines, $5 per day; that is the going rate. Someone says you cannot get men for that. In some of the more industrialized ridings, that may be true. I have heard men say they did not think they were getting enough when they were receiving board and lodging and a hundred dollars a month while working from seven o'clock in the morning until six at night. Let us be realistic about this. I know there is not another industry in Canada, and I know something about industry, that has been told by the government it must sell its products at less than the world price. When we sit down to negotiate an agreement with labour unions, the leaders point out to us that they are entitled to a reasonable profit and standard of living. I believe the hired men on the farms are entitled to give their children a good education, a good home, and have a decent standard of living. I do not believe that those of us who come from rural ridings-or those who do not for that matter -will serve their proper function in this House of Commons if they subscribe to bureaucratic control of the marketing of this product of agriculture to the extent that they make agriculture and the farmers the poor relatives of this suiper-duper form of new economy.
Last night the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that there has been no open market for Canadian wheat since 1941.

speechtext:
I would look as swanky on it probably as would the hon. member. But I am not accustomed to putting on style out in the wheat field, if I can help it; and I am not out there any more than I can help these days. I only mention that these things are relative. I am not saying for a moment that the farmers of western Canada or the farmers any place should get $3.40 for their wheat. I am not saying that at all. When we get into a war and when our boys have to do as they had to do in recent years-and as I pray to God they may not have to do again-go overseas and meet the threat, I am satisfied that something will have to be done. Many of them are now going overseas even though we hear that there is not going to be any war. I read some reports from Korea and I think as do some others in this country who think that there are signs of war. I do not believe that any class of Canadian society should take an undue advantage. Probably if there was a world shortage the minister or the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be quite justified-and he would have the support of this house-in trying to keep the price stabilized at some point that was reasonable. On the other hand, we cannot afford to let things get out of relationship by these fantastic ideologies, as a result of which production may be affected.
The Minister of Agriculture said that there is no open market. But, Mr. Speaker, there has always been a free market. There was a free market in Chicago in the United States all during those years; and so far as that is concerned, there was a world price for wheat. During the time that this government was selling wheat at $1.55 a bushel and $2 a bushel in Britain, Britain herself was paying as high as $5 a bushel for wheat from Turkey; she was paying almost that for wheat from Argentina and she got so short of wheat, after our summer fallow policy in Canada, that she bought rye at $4.08 a bushel to take the place of wheat. Who is there to say that there is no open market left in the world, except those who want to control it under bulk trading systems in this country and in other countries as well? That is why I think the time has come, when this experiment has been tried, has been found wanting and to have failed, for the Minister of Agriculture to get back to his first idea of soundness, independent of what the political consequences are. Now in the twilight of his political career I would suggest to him that there is no other man in Canada who can go out to western Canada and tell the truth to the

people there as well as he can, or with such vigour as he still has. In fact, I think he has too much to go to the other place, as the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) suggested; we want to keep him here for a while. In fact he has more vigour than any of the rest on the other side of the house. But I would suggest that he go out and use some of that vigour to tell the people of Canada the truth.
I would suggest that he say to them: "I tried to help you. I saw you selling wheat at low prices when there was no war and when we were in a world depression. I made up my mind that I would see to it that I would try to stabilize the price. I made statements out here in. political campaigns that I would do everything in my power to see that you never sold wheat for less than $1 a bushel again." With those high motives he had I would agree. But I suggest that he go out now and say: "Boys, you stood by me in the past when I was wrong. I ask you to go along with me now when I have repented and am going to be right; because I have made a mistake; I have made a failure. I have lost you half a billion dollars. There is no teacher like experience. You have paid for your experience with interest, cash on the barrelhead. You have had good crops. God gave you good ground. You paid high prices for big combines to harvest your crops fast, so you could go south in the winter if you had enough acres; and if you did not have enough acres, I paid you for summer fallowing, even." That is the position the minister could take and not get off a sound economic basis the great agricultural industry that should be the last to get off the basis of sound economy in this country. Why put it off first?
The Minister of Agriculture has twitted my friends down here to my left; but I have not heard from them anything wilder in proposals than those that have already cost this country a half a billion dollars. I will say it may have been worth it; because if the right hon. gentleman will do that, and if my hon. friends down to my left-who I know can learn fast-will have observed what has happened by this socialistic experiment, then we shall never have a socialistic government in Canada.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture gave some figures. I wish I had his department to help me get these figures together. I am not going to misquote my hon. friend; because while he often surprises me by what he says, it would be a surprise to him if I misquoted him. But he said that he got $2 a bushel and that had he not got $2 a bushel he would have had to take $1.80 a bushel; because we have gone, as you will notice, into the world sphere
Canadian Wheat Board Act now. We have an international wheat agreement now for $1.80 for the year 1949-50. The minister said that the price was $2 per bushel,-to be exact I think he said it was $2.06, because you have 6 cents for carrying charges.

The minister is only one cent out, then. That is not so bad. The Minister of Agriculture did say that had he not taken the $2.05, he would have had to take $1.80.
I know the Minister of Agriculture is smart and I know he is honest. I know that it is going to bother him, as it is going to bother me, to know why he failed to point out the fact that, so far as Canada was concerned, instead of there being 25 cents difference there was only 7 cents difference. In this particular case I would rather say he was honest than that he was smart in his trading, because it is clear that in his trading with Great Britain he has made a colossal blunder. It might be said, in the language of the street, that in this deal we have had it put over us very badly. I am inclined to think that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) went over to Great Britain and listened to the government over there tell him that they were paying $2. Then, while he was over there trying to harvest his losses, he mentioned that they gave him $28 million more than he would have got out of the international wheat agreement, when as a matter of fact the international wheat agreement, a copy of which I have here, says:
The basic minimum and maximum prices lor the duration of the agreement shall be-
And then for the year 1949-50 it gives a maximum of $1.80. And then it says that these shall be in:
-Canadian currency per bushel at the parity for the Canadian dollar, determined for the purposes of the international monetary fund as at March 1, 1949 for No. 1 Manitoba northern wheat in bulk in store Fort William/Port Arthur.
On July 6, 1946, when this agreement was drawn up, the exchange situation was such that our dollar stood at one hundred cents. On September 20, 1949, it was down by 10 per cent; and it was not until September 30, 1950, that this 10 per cent was withdrawn.
Therefore the Minister of Agriculture, despite the fact that we had understood before from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that the agreements had been settled, and while it was understood that they should have been settled on July 31 for each year preceding, made this reckless pilgrimage back to Great Britain to settle those agreements. He went back and evidently made a $20 million blunder in the consideration. He tells us now that we get $28 million

Canadian Wheat Board Act more. However, if my mathematics is correct, 10 per cent of $1.80 brings the figure up to $1.98, or almost $2 in Canadian funds.
The United Kingdom-Canadian agreement is in Canadian funds at a rate of $2, while the international wheat agreement is in United States funds. Therefore when the exchange rate was at 10 per cent it makes a difference, not of 28 cents on the $2 price, or 20 cents, but a difference of only 2 cents.

I am using it, from the figures you used. I do not want to read again what the minister said, because I know he will not want to hear it again; it is bad enough to have to listen to it once. However, what he said was not the fact-and perhaps I should not say that, because it might not be parliamentary. His statement may have been half true, and I am not saying that the minister knew the other half. But in view of the weakness of the whole deal I think one may deduce what has happened. I know that that was the general understanding.
On the other hand the Minister of Agriculture has told us about the way the agreement worked in the past. It is a big agreement, Mr. Speaker, one which deals with millions of dollars. I know that in the House of Commons it has become customary to throw a million here and a million there, and we lose some of our sense of respect for money. But, after all, I am amazed to see that one of my farmer friends would ever become as careless as the Minister of Agriculture has shown he has become.
There was involved an agreement for five years to sell our major agricultural product, an agreement involving millions upon millions of dollars. True, only 600 million of a total of 2 billion bushels was involved in the agreement; but the other wheat was sold everywhere. There was no open market, no world market. It was sold domestically sometimes below the agreement price, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), Other places it was sold for perhaps a dollar above that price. It was sold wherever the need was found. There was no organized salesmanship as there had been in earlier years. It was just a case of the minister saying, "I have wheat; come on, boys, you can have it for what you like.
I am getting so much today, and I want more; but if you are good fellows you can have it for less. We will pay a bonus on flour and tell the housewife that we have lowered the cost of living by taking it off the farmer."
I do not believe the farmers of this country should be asked to bear the loss involved in this colossal error-and I say it is a colossal 
error. I say again that it has upset the trade, and that the agreement has not been lived up to. And those who can be charged for its not being lived up to are not the British people.

speechtext:
An hon. member says, "Sure they are." Well, he who runs may read, and I suggest that the hon. member read the agreement. It says:
The actual prices to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom government and the Canadian government not later than the 31st December, 1947, and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December, 1948. In determining the prices for these two crop years, 1948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop year and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
That is why I presume that at one time the Minister of Trade and Commerce made the statement which is recorded in Hansard. Although it was revised then, it seemed to be unrevised again last night. The result is that this was supposed to have been settled. If it was not settled by agreement, then it should have been settled, and there was no authority for its not being settled-except for the fact that, as the Minister of Agriculture says, at some place in London he had a conversation. He did not say whether he was out for dinner, and I know he is too seriously-minded to' be in a cocktail lounge, or any place like that. He said that he varied the agreement verbally, and arranged for its renewal.
Mr. Speaker, that is a strange, a most unusual type of international negotiation. Here we have an agreement dealing with billions of dollars with respect to our chief product. A settlement is supposed to have been made by agreement, and concluded the year before. But Mr. Strachey and Mr. Gardiner sit down in consultation in a hotel room, or in the lobby of a hotel, or on an aeroplane, or somewhere else-even in an office-and renegotiate. "We can do this verbally"-but the agreement says it should have been settled long ago. What hope is there when we see that loose type of business being carried on? What right have we, or what right has anyone, to insinuate that the British did not keep their bargain, especially when the Minister of Agriculture was at least $28 million out in his calculations anyway?
I know there was a good deal more wheat than was sold under this agreement. I shall not labour the issue, more than to say that

I do not believe the Minister of Agriculture had any right verbally to change a contract that was of such vital concern to the economy of this nation. Whether he and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have or have not always been in unison in their thinking is a matter for conjecture. Perhaps in one sense it is none of parliament's business, so long as they stand behind the same type of policy and make the same sort of statements to the House of Commons.
It does not surprise me that the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
We asked the United Kingdom government what further settlement it is to make on account of the have regard to clause.
The United Kingdom government took a very strong position that they had fulfilled all obligations under that clause, and so far as the United Kingdom was concerned. We agreed on behalf of Canada that considering all the circumstances that was the case.
I am not going to burden the house further than to say that the Minister of Agriculture sold this bill of goods to parliament in 1946. He tried it out and it has cost the Canadian economy through the wheat producers and farmers generally well up to three-quarters of a billion dollars. He said at the time that he was not even sure of himself. We know that in his earlier years he did not believe in it. Whether he was trying to outbid the socialist trend in his native province of Saskatchewan or not, I urge him in conclusion, after having tried the experiment, to realize the one thing that is known to every financial man, businessman and farmer, that it is unsound in practice and not in keeping with business or international leadership. It has gone a long way toward creating a slight irritation between us and the motherland and has caused considerable suspicion of other countries.
I say to the minister to study carefully ways and means that will give the farmers a fair deal. After all, the farmers co-operative organizations I think have done a good job in this country. We have seen the wheat pool in action and we have seen the co-operative movements in action. They have done a pretty good job. I have never seen any cooperative organization making such an economic blunder as the co-operative organization of government which has to keep one eye on politics and which has shown such little capacity for sound business management.
