It is far less than the amount of money that was promised in the last election. Whatever the faults or merits of that decision may be, I deprecate one impression which has been created throughout Canada in recent weeks. Certain members of this house have charged that the British government is responsible for this "wheat mess" through their failure to fulfil an obligation under the British-Canadian wheat agreement. That charge is so patently dishonest and untrue that I should like to speak for a few minutes about it.
First I should like to refer briefly to the history of the British-Canadian wheat agreement. Hon. members will recall that from 1946 to 1950 western farmers suffered a loss on pretty well every bushel of wheat they sold to the wheat board. This naturally caused a certain amount of discontent. However our farmers were assured by government speakers, including the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), particularly during the last election, that at the end of the five year pool certain compensatory payments would be made to make up for some of these losses.
There has always been a good deal of vagueness as to just where that payment was going to come from. Up until the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made his now famous speech last June, most Liberal members intimated that this final payment was going to come from the rather ambiguous "have regard to" clause in the British-Canadian wheat agreement. As has been pointed out, this clause provided that any losses sustained by the farmers in the first two years of the agreement would be taken into consideration by the two governments when they were fixing the price for the third
1094

Canadian Wheat Board Act and fourth years. I think clause 2(b) of the agreement is significant. That clause reads in part:
The actual price 'to be paid for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1948-49 shall be negotiated and settled between the United Kingdom and the government of Canada not later than the 31st December, 1947, and prices for wheat to be bought and sold within the crop year 1949-50 shall be negotiated and settled not later than the 31st December 1948.
What actually happened? The price of wheat for the first two years was set at $1.55. After negotiation, as called for in the agreement, the price for the third year was set at $2. After negotiation, as the contract called for, the price in the fourth year was also set at $2. According to the British, the prices for the third and fourth years were agreed upon after having regard to Canadian losses in the first two years. The Minister of Trade and Commerce must have agreed because he said on June 5, 1950, after quoting that clause, and I -refer hon. members to page 3221 of Hansard:
That is the "have regard to" clause in the agreement. I suggest that regard was paid in fixing these prices.
This statement was made nine months ago. Meanwhile the price of wheat on the world market remained considerably higher than the farmer was receiving under -the agreement. Whether it was justified or not, there was increasing discontent throughout the west over this fact. Partly as a result of this discontent the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a trip last May to Great Britain. He took advantage of his presence there to ask the British once again for concessions under the "have regard to" clause. However the British took the position that they had fulfilled all the obligations. But, at the minister's request, they did agree to give Canada preference on wheat purchases in 1951 and 1952. It was clearly understood that this would be the final concession they would make.
When the Minister of Trade and Commerce came back he reported to the house in a lucid statement. I am going to place extracts from that speech on Hansard once again because I think the farmers of the west should have every opportunity of reading them. I quote from page 3221 of Hansard of June 5, 1950, where the minister is reported as follows:
The matter of the "have regard to" clause was discussed in great detail during our sessions with Sir Stafford Cripps and other ministers of the United Kingdom government. The whole situation was reviewed. The United Kingdom is just as positive as I have been in my statements in the house as to what the world price of wheat really was in those periods. My hon. friend said the world price was the price in a local market to which Canadian grain is not permitted access. I wonder
fMr. Thatcher.]
what the world price would have been if we had been able to ship our Canadian grain to the Chicago market, which he says is the great criterion for world prices. We went over the agreement while in London. We asked the United Kingdom government what further settlement it is to make on account of the "have regard to" clause. The United Kingdom government took a very strong position that they had fulfilled all obligations under the clause, and so far as the United Kingdom was concerned. We agreed on behalf of Canada that considering all the circumstances that was the case.
That is very definite. Last night the Minister of Agriculture suggested to this house that this statement was not the official report. Even if he is correct, what difference does it make? If we can believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce on May 29, and- I think we can, then surely we can -believe him on June 5. On June 5 he made the categorical statement that the British had fulfilled the "have regard to" clause. Last evening the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) engaged in some of the most amazing doubletalk I have seen since coming to parliament. He suggested to the house that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) did not really say what Hansard proves he did say. He said that the "period" was in the wrong place. He stated that if it had been punctuated differently then the meaning would have been different. I wonder if since -confederation a minister has ever used such a weak excuse to get out of a firm commitment? I watched the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I think he was a little embarrassed. Certainly the face of the Minister of Trade and Commerce turned red. I wonder whom the Minister of Agriculture was trying to fool.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I said a moment ago that my Liberal friends from the prairies had to find a scapegoat; so they looked around, and somebody got the idea of blaming Britain. They thought, "Why not in some way accuse the British socialist government of failing to live up to its obligations?" Well, the idea looked like manna from heaven. So notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), on June 5 last, told us that Britain had fulfilled its contract, and notwithstanding the fact that the matter had been officially closed for almost nine months, certain members of this house started what

I would suggest was an unwarranted and insidious campaign against the British government. The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) started it in a very mild way. I think perhaps he had qualms of conscience before he commenced, but he did throw out some insinuations. This is what he had to say at page 150 of Hansard:
I am going to say how pleased X am that the British government has considered fulfilling the "have regard to" clause in the five year wheat pool contract ... I am not going to mention any alternatives because I am confident the British government is sound and fair enough to see that justice is done.
I ask the hon. member for Kindersley how he can reconcile those words with the statement last June 5 of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Who told the hon. member for Kindersley the British government was ready to renegotiate this contract? It must have been the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer).
Then on February 8 that bluff party stalwart, the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott), took up the cudgels and had this to say:
I repeat that the government of Canada must impress on the government of Britain that the "have regard to" clause must be carried out.
I wonder where the hon. member for Springfield was last June 5. He could not have been in the house June 5, and yet been so far off the beam the other evening. Perhaps he was home in Manitoba.
The next speaker was the genial hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Smith). I think he was a little ashamed of himself when he made this statement, but he got it out:
I urge the government to crack the whip and get going on this negotiation or discussion with the United Kingdom and let us have a decision on what is going to happen in respect to the five year pool payments.
Did not the hon. member know that a decision had been reached by his own Minister of Trade and Commerce nine months previously, or did he not want to know?
Finally the hon. member for Maple Creek took his turn. In my opinion he is a fine gentleman, but on that occasion he made what I think was one of the most shameful speeches, and what I believe was the most anti-British speech I have ever heard in the House of Commons. Realizing full well that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had publicly acknowledged that Britain had fulfilled her obligations, nevertheless he went on to charge the British with violating a contract. Here are his words:
I believe more emphasis should be placed on the honouring of a contract between two countries.

Who has not honoured this contract? The British have. It is the Liberal members who are crying for revision of obligations long since completed. The hon. member went on:
I think the contract should be fulfilled by the people who signed it.
Does the hon. member suggest that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had no authority or power to make an agreement?
Finally the hon. member for Maple Creek addressed C.C.F. members and had this to say:
They should ask them what they are going to do about meeting the obligation they are in honour bound to meet. If they do not pay it, then I would say that there is a conspiracy between the socialists of Canada and the socialists of Great Britain to refrain from paying the farmers of western Canada what is their just due.
There is a conspiracy, all right, but it is not a conspiracy between the socialist government of Britain and the socialists of Canada. There is a conspiracy among prairie Liberal members to avoid carrying out election promises, and to foist the blame on a friendly commonwealth country. So one by one they joined the chorus.
Then at the height of the campaign one week end the Minister of Agriculture sneaked out of Ottawa and made a dramatic trip to Great Britain to try to argue with the stubborn British. According to rumour, most of his cabinet colleagues were not very keen about the trip. After all, most of them took the position that "a deal is a deal"-particularly when it is in writing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill which we are theoretically discussing at the moment provides for three amendments to the wheat board act. I am in favour of those amendments, and from what I have been able to hear I believe they meet with the general approval of the house. When we reach the committee stage, however, there are a few questions I should like to ask in connection with the price which is going to be established for the settlement of any particular pool.
This debate has not been on these three amendments, but has been confined almost entirely to the five year wheat pool or the four year wheat agreement, as it has been called. I should first like to make a few

comments on the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) last night. I was really rather surprised at that speech. To begin with, I would compliment him by saying that he gave us an extremely agile display of mental gymnastics and verbal legerdemain. He started with a little history of the wheat board act, but it was of course his own brand of history and given strictly from his own point of view. In the end it turned out to be what I would call his own brand of political pseudo-history designed to confuse the subject rather than illuminate it.
The minister's speech, Mr. Speaker, -can be divided into two main parts. Everything he said falls into one part or the other, although he did at times become a little confused between the two contentions he was trying to put forward. I was amazed at the manner in which he moved from one part of the speech to the other without giving any indication that either of these two parts contradicted the other. Apparently from the loudness of his voice when he was putting forth these contentions, he was convinced that we would not think they were either. Listening to the minister talk in this way, a couplet came into my mind. I believe it is from Scott's "Lay of the Last Minstrel". It seems to me to be quite apt, and the couplet runs as follows:
That through a bog, from hag to hag,
Could bound like any Billhope stag.
I may say that the word "hag" as used by Scott in this couplet means a firm piece of ground situated in a swamp. The minister was certainly floundering in a swamp of his own making. He certainly gave a great exhibition of jumping from one position to another in that swamp. However, Mr. Speaker, I do not think he was on very firm ground in either position in which he landed.
I should like to analyse this speech to some extent. In the first part of his speech the minister tried to prove that Britain had not lived up to the four year contract, and that any losses that the farmers had suffered were entirely Britain's fault. That was the whole thesis, and the attempt was to place the blame in Britain. The roar from the Liberal benches which greeted a contention of that kind by the member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) evidently indicates that most of the Liberal members who were in the house take that position, and are going to do their best to push it. When we come to the second part of the minister's speech, we find it was an argument that Britain had lived up to the have regard to clause, which is exactly the opposite of the argument that he was making in the first part of his speech. He said she had lived up to the have regard to clause to the extent of $35 million and that the $65

million, which as the minister said was now being paid into the wheat pool on Britain's account and which was a doubtful statement with which I shall deal later, would make up $100 million. He said that gave the wheat producers a satisfactory price for their wheat, and one which they were not entitled to complain about. Here is what he had to say about the satisfactory price as recorded at page 1068 of Hansard:
The payments made to the farmers when completed will amount to an average of $1.82 a bushel from the five year pool. Now I would ask members of this house this question: How much more equitable can a price be made?
How much better could it be? In other words, he is doing his best to prove that the farmer got all he was entitled to receive, which was just the opposite of what he sought to prove in the first part of his speech. A little farther down on the same page he said:
The payments made to farmers when completed will amount to $1.82 a bushel. This is two cents above the figure which has been written into the international wheat agreement as satisfactory to farmers.
Referring to the same thing a little later he said:
This contract, this pool, brought the farmers for the last five years two cents a bushel more than that. What criticism could there be made of it? As a matter of fact there is nothing in connection with that to criticize.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if the second part of the minister's speech is accurate, and the facts which I have just quoted are accurate, then necessarily the first part of his speech must be wrong. The only purpose then of the first part of his speech is to stir up, I would say quite incorrectly and unnecessarily, bad feeling toward Britain on the part of our western wheat farmers. That is the only purpose it could serve. So far as I can see, that must be the only reason he made it, unless he admits that the second part of his speech is incorrect and the first part is the one he wants to stand by.
This business of stirring up bad feeling towards Britain is exactly what has been done by the speech the minister made last night and by similar statements made by the minister and others of his party. They have stirred up that bad feeling. I think there is no doubt about it, Mr. Speaker, that they are mischievous statements which were made for purely political reasons and in an attempt to turn the anger of the wheat growers from the minister and the government to the British people and to the British government. On the other hand, if there is any force in the minister's contention and in the contention of his followers to the effect that Britain was entirely responsible for the losses the
Canadian Wheat Board Act farmers suffered, then of course, conversely, the second part of the speech must be wrong and the wheat growers have not had a fair deal. This is what we recommended last year. We asked that the interests of Canada should have priority over the interests of any other country. Some of us from British Columbia were accused, we think unfairly, of having carried on a filibuster against other bills last year. We are rather proud of that because I know how pleased the people in the Fraser valley are about this and I have good reason to know how pleased the people of British Columbia are. This result is mainly due to the efforts put forth last year by a few members from that province. We asked that at least the main oil or gas line should be within Canada.
This particular bill deals with a gas line. It is expected that other pipe line bills will be coming before the committee. Those of us who have been successful in promoting the development of our province are not going to be stampeded by anyone into not giving mature consideration to the best interests of our province. Incidentally, any gas or oil line that enters British Columbia must pass through my riding, so I do not care two hoots which company it is that is building the line.
We want these bills to go before the committee in the regular manner when the sponsor of the bill can give whatever information is asked for. The members for British Columbia already have an amendment prepared providing that the main line must go through Canada. If that is known it will take

less time for the sponsor to explain his bill and how the building of the line is going to be financed. The sponsor of a bill should be prepared to come before a committee and state that the company is ready to build up Canada first. There should always be foremost in our minds the realization that it is our duty to protect the interests of our province. Again I want to commend the sponsor of this particular bill and his backers. Mr. Speaker, before the bill is read the third time I should like to say a few words. I want to make it quite clear that I am not objecting to the bill on technological grounds. However, there are two things that I have against it. The first is that the capital

to sponsor the project is 100 per cent American. Second, in order to line up the project there appeared before the standing committee United States engineers who have done the surveying from one end of the country to the other. We had United States technicians and banking experts give evidence before that committee. It struck me during the discussion that there is some lack of interest or confidence on the part of Canadian capital. Practically ever since I came into the house we have been selling our resources for development by United States capital. In my opinion that is not a good thing. I think it shows a lack of initiative on the part of Canadian capital and a lack of interest on the part of the government. I feel, and always have felt, that if we are going to build Canada for Canadians and create a status of nationhood our basic resources should be developed and controlled within this country.
The second thing I am concerned about- and I expressed this fear in the committee -is that the pipe line will pipe natural gas from Alberta as far as Quebec city. I am not unmindful of the fact, and I reminded the committee, that the basic industry in Nova Scotia is coal. Natural gas is a competitor of coal. If the pipe line is going to tap Quebec city and Montreal, if it is going to be successful in entering that area, it is going to replace the market for maritime coal. That may not happen within the next year or two but in the foreseeable future if that pipe line is going to justify its existence in that area then so far as I am concerned it will have to replace the fuel being used there at the present time.
Natural gas is definitely adapted to domestic use. I am safe in saying there are a million and a half tons of maritime coal being used in the Quebec and greater Montreal areas at the present time for domestic purposes. Natural gas can be used in any industry with the exception of the steel industry, and in the areas I have just mentioned there is a large percentage of maritime coal being used for metallurgical and industrial purposes. The standing committee heard the chairman of the dominion coal board, Mr. Uren. He said that no representations had been made to him on the part of the Nova Scotia or New Brunswick coal industries. I can understand that. These bills come in through the back door from the other place. We get them and there is not much time to consider them. That will not be an advance if it destroys the very base of the economy of another province. So I suggest that before this matter is finally decided the government consider what may happen if this fuel is permitted to go into Montreal and down as far as Quebec, taking over an area which is very important to an industry in which the government has a considerable investment.
I have no desire to hold up the bill. As far as I can see it is one of the best pipe line bills to come before the house. I was a member of the committee, and the financial experts, engineers and other witnesses appearing before that committee were extremely competent. They had all the facts at their fingertips and there was no doubt as to their ability and experience in projects of this kind. And of course they did write in the proviso that the main trunk line was to be all-Canadian; and they satisfied every desire of the committee as to their honesty and integrity in that respect. At the same time I did raise this question, because it seemed to me I would be lax in my duty if I did not, seeing the development of competition to the fuels produced in the province from which I come. If this competing fuel is brought into the areas which are important to my province it can undersell United States anthracite by at least $1 a ton, and I think it will do the same at least to bituminous coal. So I want the Minister of Trade and Commerce to think this over. If the investment the government has made in the mining industry of Nova Scotia is to be threatened by developments of this kind, at least something should be planned for that part of the country which will suffer as a result of this technological advance.

He said: In moving second reading of the bill it should not be necessary to take up too much of the time of the house, particularly since we find the principles relating to the second reading of private bills set out in Beauchesne's third edition, citation 740, at page 280:
The house, in reading a private bill for the second time, decides that the matter involved is one which may be looked into by the committee. It is only in case that an exceptional principle is enunciated that the second reading is refused.
Then citation 771 reads:
Mr. J. W. Lowther, chairman of committees of ways and means, of the British house, speaking on the subject on February 25, 1926, said:	"The rule
which the house had generally followed, and, he thought, very wisely, had been to allow the second reading of private bills to go through unless any strikingly new principle happened to be enunciated therein, and in such cases the house must pause before it accepts the principle."
Citation 769 reads in part:
The second reading of a private bill corresponds with the same stage in other bills, and in agreeing to it the house affirms the general principle, or expediency, of the measure. There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee. Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable, the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee.
I might also read citation 770:
The house does not profess to decide upon the second reading as to the truth or otherwise of the allegations of fact upon which a proposed bill is based, and in conceding a second reading to a private bill, the house is regarded as merely giving its sanction to its general principle on the hypothesis that the committee to which it is afterward referred finds those allegations proved. It is usual, therefore, to allow a second reading except where the bill enunciates some principle which the house is not prepared to affirm.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had just been making a short analysis of the speech delivered last night by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), pointing out particularly that the first half of his speech was flatly contradicted by the last half of it. Just when the house rose I had been saying something about the row, so to speak, which developed here over the statement made in the house on June 5, 1950, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and which had to do with the placing of commas, periods and things of that sort, and whether bound Hansard and the daily edition were the same or not. All of these things amount to nothing. They are trifling and piffling. However, there is one thing which appears evident from all of the discussion on that point, and that is that the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on June 5, 1950-and which I shall not quote again-made it abundantly clear to the members of this house and to the people of Canada that, as far as he was concerned, the four year agreement with Great Britain was closed and the thing was over. The point which is so clear is that, of course, it is at direct variance with the contention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in the first part of his speech last night, which was more or less to the effect that Canada never had agreed that the deal was closed, that his trip to England a short time ago was quite in order, and so on.
I would make one final comment in that connection, and it is this: If all that the Minister of Agriculture said last night is correct, then why did the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) make the statement he did make on June 5 last? The two things do not jibe; they are definitely and directly opposed to one another.

There was another matter brought into the discussion last night by the Minister of Agriculture, and that was the international wheat agreement price, and a comparison of the price received in the last two years of the British wheat agreement with the price set under the international wheat agreement.
The minister contended that the have regard to clause in the British wheat agreement had been met by the fact that the Canadian farmers had received $35 million more under the British agreement than they would have under the international agreement. Of course he was careful to qualify that immediately, by saying that the change in the exchange rates had brought that down to a net amount to the farmer of $16 million. The farmers are not particularly interested in the exchange rate; the thing that does appeal to them, and that they know something about, and that will add force, is that they have not got that $35 million in their pockets, and they are not going to get it.
In other words, any talk about $35 million secured in that way does not mean anything, from a practical point of view. The farmers have not got it. And further to that point, the price received by the farmers under the British wheat agreement should be related to what might be called the general world price rather than to the international wheat agreement price. Under the world market price the farmers not only do not gain anything, but they lost further on that deal.
There is one other thing I should like to mention briefly. As reported at page 1069 of Hansard, the minister was speaking in connection with a statement made by numerous people in regard to the losses the farmers had suffered from the sale of their wheat. This is what he said:
The argument is a ridiculous attempt to mislead farmers, and it is used only for that purpose.
That is a statement the minister should not have made. It was brought into question by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). However, the minister did make that statement, and I should like to take this opportunity of throwing it right back in his face. That statement of the minister applies to a much greater extent to the statements he made last night in connection with wheat, and the wheat deal, generally, than it does to the statements made by farmers throughout the country as to the losses they have suffered under the deal.
The more one listens to the Minister of Agriculture discussing wheat, the more confused one becomes, unless he sets against the minister's statement a little common-sense knowledge of what the situation has actually been. As a matter of fact, once one
Canadian Wheat Board Act leaves what might be described as the narrow, tortuous and dark alleys of the minister's reasoning, and emerges out on the broad highway of plain common-sense thinking, the facts of the wheat agreement become quite simple, and there is no need for any confusion about them.
At the risk of some repetition, I shall recapitulate briefly. First, the wheat deal was made with Great Britain for the first two years at a price of $1.55 a bushel. No one disputes that; and the have regard to clause was written in, so far as the price to be paid for the last two years was concerned.
The minister himself put on record what was said by the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, in connection with the subsequent agreement which was made for the second two years. The agreement was that the wheat would be paid for at the rate of $2 a bushel. Since that time the British have claimed that this new contract price of $2 a bushel settled the have regard to clause along with, as a matter of fact, their agreement to take more than they were really required to take under the new international wheat agreement.
I have already spoken about the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the house, that to all intents and purposes the four year wheat contract was closed. The British were not going to pay any more on it, and the Canadian government-while he did not say they were satisfied-had accepted it. Those are the basic facts, to begin with. Subsequent to that the Minister of Agriculture has done everything he possibly could to build up in western Canada the idea that the low price received by farmers was due entirely to what has been represented as the niggardly, if not dishonest, attitude of the British government.
The project to build up this idea, the attempt to sell it to the western farmers, has been done for very obvious political reasons. It is done entirely in an attempt to draw away from the Minister of Agriculture and the government the responsibility for entering into an extremely poor deal, and to direct the anger of the farmers to the British government and the British people instead of to themselves. In other words, they are trying to get out from under, by means of that argument.
The aotual fact of the situation is this: the dominion government-the government we have before us-made this wheat deal, and is thus responsible for the loss the farmers have suffered under it. Nobody else is responsible for it. What happened was that they made a colossal error in judgment. They thought the price was going to go up; instead

Canadian Wheat Board Act of that it went down. As a result of that every farmer who grows wheat in the west is dissatisfied with the price he has received.

As I said, I do not want to go into the estimating business, but there is no question that extensive losses have been incurred.

For some years the government defended its wheat agreement in this house and throughout the country on the basis that it gave an assured long-term market, not only for wheat but also for other farm products, in Great Britain. Even as late as 1947 the

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, March 2, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) announced that the final payment on the British wheat agreement would be 8-3 cents a bushel. Since that time a great deal of bitterness has been generated in western Canada, and I think only naturally, because the farmers of western Canada feel that there has been a very definite breach of contract in so far as the have regard to clause is concerned, either a

breach of contract or a breach of faith, whichever you like to call it. Various farm organizations and wheat pools have asked that a payment of 25 cents a bushel should be made. I think that request is a very moderate one and fully justified in the face of all the circumstances because the total loss to the farmers was, as a matter of fact, considerably in excess of 25 cents a bushel over the last five years.
Many persons today are endeavouring to discredit the wheat board as the 100 per cent marketing agent for wheat on the ground that the board is responsible for these losses. I would say that the vast majority of the farmers are solidly behind the wheat board as the marketing agency because they realize that it is not responsible for these losses but that the responsibility rests fairly and squarely upon the shoulders of the Canadian government.
I say that for two main reasons. First, it was the Canadian government that signed the British wheat agreement. Moreover-and this is an important point-it was the Canadian government that agreed to ignore the contract under the have regard to clause. Second, the government compelled the wheat board to sell wheat to the Canadian millers at considerably less than the price of class II wheat. In that way they of course have subsidized Canadian consumers. I would say it was largely as a result of these policies that the western agricultural conference at Saskatoon, January 20 to 22, 1949, passed the following resolution which I will quote in part:
. . . that the Canadian wheat board should be an agency operating in the interests of grain producers, with a duty at all times to sell grain for the best available price whether in export or domestic markets, and should not be used as an instrument of government policy to limit domestic prices.
In other words, they feel the wheat board should be allowed to sell wheat for the highest price they can get, and if it becomes the policy of the government to subsidize the Canadian consumer then the government should pay that cost and not pass it on to the Canadian farmer.

Because we have discussed it time and again. I have been to various conventions just the same as the minister, and I know very well what they had in mind. A committee came down here to meet us on the very question, and that was the point they made. They did not want a repetition of what had happened under the wheat policy whereby the government forced the farmers to accept the cost of subsidizing the Canadian consumers. They did not want similar action in the handling of coarse grains. They made it very clear when they met us.
First of all I want to take the question of the losses under the British wheat agreement. On the basis of class II wheat the loss, as shown by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), totalled $431 million in round figures. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has argued that we supported the agreement because we thought that prices would fall in the later years. Of course the present Minister of Trade and Commerce was not in charge of the department at the time the agreement was signed. His predecessor took a very different stand. He took the stand that we should not ask our former allies to pay the maximum price for wheat. He took the stand that there was a moral obligation on our part to allow our allies to have wheat at less than the world price. At that time we stated that if there was a moral obligation on Canada to allow our former allies to have wheat at less than the world market price then that was the responsibility of the Canadian people, and the Canadian people should pay the cost and not try to pass it on to the Canadian farmers as the government is apparently trying to do today. A year later when the British wheat agreement was introduced we discussed it in this house on the 27th of February, 1947. That was the first time we had an opportunity to discuss it, and at that time I had this to say.
In the early part of this agreement the farmer is making a considerable sacrifice. He is losing anywhere from 50 cents to 75 cents a bushel.
I was very conservative at that time. I went on:
If in the next two or three years there is a wheat shortage, if crops are poor, the price of wheat will be maintained at probably a high level and will remain there. Then the guarantee becomes absolutely useless. If that should be the situation over the next two or three years the farmers of this country, as a result of this agreement, are going to lose several hundred million dollars. I believe that the wheat agreement with Britain was fully justified, but it does entail in its early stages a considerable sacrifice on the part of our farmers. We feel that the sacrifice should be borne by the people of Canada as a whole.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
Exactly what I pointed out at that time has come about; and as we felt then, we still feel that any loss suffered as a result of allowing our allies in Great Britain to have cheap wheat should be borne by the Canadian people as a whole, not only by the Canadian farmer. However, the real safeguard in the British wheat agreement was the have regard clause; or we thought it was, and it should have been and I believe could have been. We have heard statements to that effect made by members of the British house when on this side, and evidently the full portent of the agreement was fully understood. I want to quote statements made by John Strachey and Sir Stafford Cripps in regard to this clause. In a speech to the Canadian club at Winnipeg on February 26, 1947, Right Hon. John Strachey, the British food minister, after quoting the latter part of clause 2(b), which is the have regard clause, stated:
Now these words mean neither more nor less than they say. They mean that the fact that we have bought our wheat from you this year below world prices-and that we may do so again next year-will be one of the factors in negotiating the actual prices to be paid in the third and fourth years. I and my government, and I am quite sure that this applies also to the Canadian government, would resist any attempt to add to or to subtract from this clear and definite statement as written into paragraph two subsection (b) of the wheat agreement.
Then in 1949, in an interview given the Canadian Press in London on February 23, Sir Stafford Cripps said:
As regards wheat we shall continue to depend on Canada for the greater part of our supplies. The four year contract negotiated in 1946 will expire in 1950 and we have recently agreed upon a price of $2 a bushel for the 1949-50 season. We think there is every possibility of the world price falling below the $2 level before the end of the contract either because of the general improvement in the supply position or as a condition of any international wheat agreement which may be concluded in the near future. If this should be the case, the Canadian farmer will enjoy a favoured position by virtue of the fixed price on which we have agreed. This might prove to be a fair compensation for the earlier years when he was selling us wheat at below the world price; it depends, of course, upon how far prices actually fall. But in any case we have agreed to discuss this matter further with the Canadian government some time toward the middle of 1950.
What happened when the representatives of the two countries met to deal with this question referred to by Sir Stafford Cripps? I apologize to the house for repeating what has been read so many times, but in view of the fact that I want to tie another statement to it I feel obliged to quote once more what was said in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) on June 5, 1950, in regard to the agreement reached last year. I want to be very careful about my

Canadian Wheat Board Act punctuation and I am quoting from page 3221 of Hansard for last year:
We went over the agreement while in London. We asked the United Kingdom government what further settlement it is to make on account of the have regard to clause. The United Kingdom took a very strong position that they had fulfilled all obligations under that clause, and so far as the United Kingdom was concerned. We agreed on behalf of Canada that considering all the circumstances that was the case.
The strange point is that the Minister of Trade and Commerce and especially the Minister of Agriculture do not appear to think that was a fair statement. I have always regarded the Minister of Trade and Commerce as a very responsible individual and I do not think that he would get up in this house and make irresponsible statements. Certainly if he made a mistake in unrevised Hansard he could have changed it in revised Hansard; and if he still found that he had made a mistake he could have done as the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew) did and made a very long correction a few days later. But he did not attempt to do so. Therefore I think we are justified in saying that statement represents what the minister really meant at the time.
I say that for another reason. I think that is actually what happened. I have a press report I am going to read, but before dping so I want to mention the fact that the Minister of Agriculture said he had discussed that statement with some of the British officials and pointed out that it was made during the committee stage, and that they had never referred to it after that. Let me remind him that they are referring to it now. They are making a statement very similar to that made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am quoting now from the Edmonton Journal of Wednesday, February 28. The clipping refers to a question asked the chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. Gaitskell, by Colonel Crosthwaite-Eyre, regarding the amount of the payment to be made to Canada in the final settlement of the wheat agreement. The reply by Mr. Gaitskell was as follows:
The matter was fully discussed in May, 1950, with Mr. Howe, and the result is that no further payment is to be made.
So apparently as far as they are concerned an agreement was definitely reached in May, 1950, and as a result of that meeting no further payment was to be made. Of course that is directly in line with the statement made in this house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in June.
Many people are asking how such an understanding could have been reached in view of all the circumstances. What was Britain's argument as to why no further payments
fMr. Ouelch.]
should be made? This was the situation. In the third year of the agreement the price of class 2 wheat was $2.23, as recorded in the report of the wheat board. The price paid by Britain was $2, so in the third year we actually lost 23 cents a bushel. In the fourth year, as a result of the international wheat agreement, we may say, the price was $1.80 in U.S.A. funds. Britain paid us $2, so actually we gained 20 cents per bushel in the fourth year. But we had lost 23 cents per bushel in the third year, so we may say that in the third and fourth years the losses and gains balanced, though actually the losses were greater. That is all right as far as the third and fourth years are concerned; but what about the have regard clause under which in settling the final price consideration would be given to the losses suffered in the first two years? In those two years the losses amounted to $375,618,000 according to figures in the wheat board report; a full statement has been put on Hansard by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). That is based upon class 2 wheat. What was Britain's argument at that time in refusing to make any payment in regard to that $375 million? That is a question I think should be explained in this house at some time.

Now, what possible decision can there be for asking that the farmers stand

the full amount of these losses, unless it is to be part of a general stabilization plan? I am satisfied that the farmers would be quite willing to forget about any further payment, in so far as subsidizing the Canadian consumer is concerned, if in return prices are to be stabilized at a fair level in the future. After all, the farmers were asked to take a price below the world price during the war as part of the government's general stabilization program in return for which they were guaranteed that there would be stabilization in the future. We do not have that guarantee in any legislation, because it is not so stated in the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I am very glad that we have that act, and I think it is a good act. I still think, and I believe the Minister of Agriculture will agree that there needs to be further clarification of that point as to just what the basis of the support prices will be. He knows that the federation of agriculture has asked that it should be based upon parity. The federation of agriculture has agreed to meet with the minister or with the government and help to formulate a basis for a parity year, but to date that has not been done; and until it is done, agricultural price support is an uncertain quantity.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EARLY DISTRIBUTION OF PAYMENTS AT END OF POOL PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
As I say, not only have we not had a stabilization program put into operation, but we found that when the price of wheat was set in 1950-that is, when the initial payment was made in 1950-at $1.40, the minister refused to set it any higher because he said that it represented the floor price and he did not want to take the chance of having a loss. Surely if this was to be part of a stabilization program, then in view of the tremendous losses that had been suffered by the farmers in the past, they would have been justified in expecting a higher initial payment than $1.40.
But the minister stated that he was not prepared at that time to put it higher because it might mean a loss if the price of wheat fell; and he was not prepared to adopt any policy that might result in a loss to the government. I know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) thinks that the farmers during the last five years have had a better price for wheat than they have ever had before. But that is only half the story. It is no good talking about the farmers having bad a better price during this past five years than they ever had before unless at the same time you also stress the fact that their costs of production were also higher than they had even been before. The two are definitely tied together, and you cannot separate them. If you go back twenty years, you can readily see why many farmers felt that they should

nave been allowed the highest price they could get during the war; because during the depression years, during those ten years when prices went so low-for instance, in 1932 the price of wheat fell to 19J cents a bushel- the farmers were told time and again that they could not expect to get a higher price than the world price. But what happened when the war came along? Prices rose slightly during the first three years of the war; then in 1942 the government heavily increased taxation. Then the farmers found themselves in the peculiar position of having to pay an income tax on the repayment of losses incurred as a result of having to sell their produce at prices far below the cost of production. Then a few years later prices rose higher. At just about the time that prices got really good-when the farmers thought, now, here is the real chance to recover the losses we suffered during the depression years-the government put a ceiling on farm prices. I think the farmers are justified in saying: All right, you cannot have it both ways. If we have got to accept the world price in the depression years, we are entitled to the world price when prices are high. The government decided not to allow the farmers to have world prices during the war. But in return they guaranteed them that in the future they would have stabilized prices. The farmers expected the government to live up to that promise. But so far there is not much assurance that the government intends to do so. First of all, they tried to get rid of the agricultural price support. They had a resolution on the order paper to end it this parliament. But I am glad to say they reinstated it; but it is still of a nebulous character.
I want to say a few words with regard to the international wheat agreement. Personally I am much in favour of a long-term international wheat agreement and I believe that the farm organizations support it; but they expect that when an international agreement is signed, the payment should be on a sound basis. I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be the first to admit that the method of payment under the international wheat agreement is not on a sound basis. I heard him speak in Calgary. He said he did not like selling wheat a year ahead of delivery.
What is the payment under the international wheat agreement? It provides for a ceiling of $1.80 a bushel for four years. Then it provides that the floor will be dropped ten cents in each year; $1.40 the first year, $1.30 the second year, $1.20 the third year and $1.10 the fourth year. Why should the floor under wheat drop if everything else is going up?
Canadian Wheat Board Act Why should the ceiling be held down at any given level if everything else is going up? Why should the price of wheat be frozen in a case of that kind?
We are not just being wise at the present moment on this point. Back in 1948, when the international agreement was then being discussed in this house, we argued that the price under the international wheat agreement should be tied to the price level; that is, in the first year you agree upon the payment or price that is to be paid; then in subsequent years, those payments should be tied to your price level so that if the price level goes up 10 per cent, the price of wheat goes up 10 per cent; or if the price level goes down 10 per cent, then the price of wheat goes down 10 per cent. In that way you would have the price of wheat tied to the general price level. In other words, you could very well have a parity price. I should like to quote what I said in this house on February 27, 1948, when we were discussing wheat policy. As reported as page 1694 of Hansard I said:
The grain trade have used the British wheat agreement as the basis upon which to attack the principle of long term international agreements. They forget that the British wheat agreement was not a straight business deal, but was in part to help our allies, as was indicated at the time the minister brought down his early wheat legislation; therefore all the Canadian people should have stood the cost of the sacrifice and the farmers should not be expected to bear the burden. The grain trade criticized the long term agreements between countries on the grounds that whilst a certain price might be fair today it might be out of line tomorrow due to a rise or fall in the price level. That is true, and that is why we have argued that when prices are agreed upon they should be tied to the price level of the country with which the agreement is made. Then, if the price level rises the price of wheat will rise and vice versa if the price level falls. The result of that would be of course that our wheat would always bring back the same amount of imports. It would help to insulate the Canadian economy against fluctuation in world prices.
We still feel the same way. We feel that any long-term agreements that are signed should be signed on that basis. First of all agree to a price which both parties are satisfied with and then tie that price to the general price level so that it will fluctuate with the price level. Otherwise you are bound to have happen what happened under the British wheat agreement where the government guessed wrong or to have a situation similar to that we are having under the present international wheat agreement where everything else is going up and yet the price of wheat is tied down.

If you are on a bilateral basis, there would be no difficulty. You would have the price level of the country you are dealing with and you would be trading goods for goods. If their price level went up, then of course they would be paying you more and you would be paying a higher price for their goods in turn but your imports and exports would balance in that regard. If the minister would prefer not to relate it to the price level of the importing nation, it could be tied up to the general price level. But I think it should be tied to the price level of the importing country so that you can balance your trade on a bilateral basis. I know that the minister has a different view from mine on the question of multilateral trade. I believe there is a responsibility on the part of the exporting nation to see to it that the credit it establishes in any country is cleared either by importing goods from that country or by trading that credit to some other country in return for goods.
There has been a good deal of comparison between the agricultural policies of this country and the agricultural policies in the United States. I was quite interested in a statement that appeared in the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of February 23, 1951, which reads as follows:
The United States government policy provides for farm price supports not only for wheat but for a whole range of key farm products. The investment in farm price support was over $4 billion last summer in that country and the limit has been raised to $61 billion. If Canada wants to make a comparative investment in farm price supports on a population basis, the total would be nearly $600 million. The actual Canadian government investment for such a purpose has been less than $10 million.
Now, in conclusion I should like to make one brief reference to a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) when he spoke in the house yesterday. I agree with much that the minister said. In fact, the first part of his speech built up a very strong argument for the carrying out of the have regard to clause. Then, strangely enough, toward the end he reversed his stand completely and took the stand that there


should not be any further payments from Great Britain, because he tried to show that the price of wheat in the world pool was $1.82 and that the price under the British wheat agreement was $1.82, and that they balanced, after the $65 million had been added to the British wheat agreement. So according to the argument of the Minister of Agriculture that $65 million balances the price of wheat in the world pool and in the British wheat agreement pool.
The minister's statement as it is reported at page 1068 of Hansard is:
The British contract, as it has been settled with the payment of $65 million, brings $1.82 into the pool. The sale of wheat to Canadians, and all other people outside the British contract, brought $1.82 a bushel into the pool.
Then the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) asked this question:
Does that $1.82 include the ICO million bushels sold on the domestic market?
To that the minister replied:
Oh yes, it does.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me perfectly fantastic that you would include wheat sold for domestic consumption in the world price of wheat. The stand taken by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is very different; he took the opposite stand. I should like to quote what he said on June 5, 1950, as it is reported at page 3184 of unrevised Hansard. He was discussing the world price for wheat, and said:
It seems to me the price at which the bulk of the wheat is bought and paid for might well be regarded as the world price, and I therefore suggest that it would be much more reasonable to call the price under the United Kingdom-Canada agreement the world price than the price quoted on the Chicago exchange. The latter was merely a domestic price-
He said it would not be fair to call the Chicago market price the world price, because it is just a domestic price. Yet here the Minister of Agriculture includes the price of wheat sold for domestic consumption in Canada, and calls it the world price. Those two ministers had better get together.

The general purposes of the proposed amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935, are as follows:
1.	To authorize the regulation by the Canadian wheat board of the interprovincial and export trade in wheat for the purpose of meeting the requirements of the wheat contract with the United Kingdom;
2.	To make a corresponding adjustment in the pool period in relation to the wheat contract with the United Kingdom;
3.	To make necessary changes in the provisions fixing the price to be paid to producers of wheat by the Canadian wheat board;
4.	To permit the board with the special approval of the governor in council to deal in grains other-than wheat.
With respect to wheat, the proposed amendments authorize the regulation of the interprovincial and export trade in wheat by the board and the conduct of all such trading through the board until July 31, 1950. In regard to other grains, the amendment enables the board, with the approval of the governor in council, to buy, sell, and deal in other grains.
In addition to making provision for implementing the wheat contract with the United Kingdom, the proposed amendments provide for a five year pool period from August 1, 1945, until July 31, 1950, during which time producers of wheat are guaranteed a fixed initial price of $1.35 a bushel.

I think that is correct. The farmers were tied to it when other controls were taken off. If there is any doubt about it, I shall just read the report which appears in one of the daily newspapers. It reads as follows:
The three prairie wheat pools said the federal government should assume full responsibility for the obligation contained in the adjustment clause of the Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement.
In addition, the pools called for payment of $48 million to cover losses which it said wheat growers suffered because of the government's wartime domestic wheat subsidy policy.
Boards of the wheat pools of Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba met to consider the federal government's announcement last week that a final payment of 8-3 cents a bushel will be made under the five-year wheat pool. A statement said:
"The Canadian wheat pools are of the opinion that the final payment announced of 8-3 cents per bushel on 1,428,000 bushels of wheat, delivered by farmers to the 1945-49 pool, cannot be considered a satisfactory one.
"The proposed payment only partially meets what we believe to be the United Kingdom commitment under the 'have regard to' clause of the contract, and it should not be forgotten that during the period March 1, 1945, to February 17, 1947, approximately 160,000,000 bushels of wheat were used for domestic consumption and western farmers subsidized the consumer to the extent of 30 cents on every bushel of wheat used during the period.

"Producers subsidized the price from $1.55 down to $1.25 and the federal government subsidized it further from $1.25 to 77g cents. This policy provided a direct subsidy of $48 million to the Canadian consumer by the western farmer.
"In other words, the federal government adopted a subsidy policy for wheat and assessed $48 million of the cost to the wheat producers of western Canada.
"It is fully appreciated that the Canadian government has exercised strong pressure to obtain further funds from the British government in accordance with the terms of the wheat agreement between the two nations.
"It is regrettable that these efforts were unsuccessful, particularly in view of the high prices Great Britain was willing to pay to other countries and that Canada received from other countries during the same period.
"The wheat farmers of western Canada should not be made to suffer through the failure of the British government to fulfil the terms of the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement as it was interpreted to them by cabinet ministers of both the United Kingdom and Canada.
